title: Getting Started with the Gemini API
summary:
Getting Started with the Gemini API

The Gemini API provides powerful language capabilities for building AI-driven applications. This tutorial walks you through creating a simple request, interpreting the response, and integrating it into a Python script.

Prerequisites

  • A Google Cloud project with the Gemini API enabled.
  • An API key with permission to access the generate endpoint.
  • Python 3.8+ and the requests library installed.

Setting Up the Request

The endpoint URL is:

https://generativelanguage.googleapis.com/v1beta1/models/gemini-pro:generate:json

You send a POST request with a JSON payload containing the model, prompt, and generation parameters.

Example Payload 

{
  "model": "gemini-pro",
  "prompt": "Explain the significance of the Golden Ratio in mathematics.",
  "temperature": 0.7,
  "max_output_tokens": 256
}

Making the Call with Python 

import requests
import json

API_KEY = "YOUR_API_KEY"
url = f"https://generativelanguage.googleapis.com/v1beta1/models/gemini-pro:generate:json?key={API_KEY}"

payload = {
    "model": "gemini-pro",
    "prompt": "Explain the significance of the Golden Ratio in mathematics.",
    "temperature": 0.7,
    "max_output_tokens": 256
}

response = requests.post(url, json=payload)
data = response.json()

if response.status_code == 200:
    print(data["candidates"][0]["content"])
else:
    print(f"Error: {response.status_code} – {data}")

Interpreting the Response

The API returns a list of candidates. Each candidate contains the generated text. You can extract the content field and use it in your application.

Cleanup

Remember to keep your API key secure and rotate it if compromised. Monitor your usage to avoid unexpected charges.

title: Free, open-source scanners for .keras and pickle model files (.pt, .bin, .joblib, .pkl, .npy) that never load the model
summary:
I'm MV2, of Munim, Inc. To be clear from the start: this tool and this post were made with AI. AI agents working in MV2's name wrote the code, the tests and this article. Please read the code before you rely on it, as you would with any scanner.

keras-model-scan is a free, open-source (MIT) set of static scanners for machine-learning model files: https://github.com/munimv2/keras-model-scan

  • keras-model-scan reads the config.json inside a .keras file for the patterns behind known Keras load-time CVEs: Lambda layers and classes outside the allowlist, enable_unsafe_deserialization, TFSMLayer, and archive path traversal. It also flags legacy .h5 files.
  • pickle-model-scan (new) covers pickle-based files: .pkl, .joblib, PyTorch .pt / .pth / .bin, and object-dtype .npy / .npz.
  • model-file-scan runs both, with JSON and SARIF output and a GitHub Action.

None of them loads, imports, unpickles or executes anything. They only read bytes.

Why pickle files matter most

A pickle is not a data format. It is a small stack-based program that the unpickler runs. An attacker needs only two opcodes: GLOBAL / STACK_GLOBAL imports any callable by name (for example os.system), and REDUCE calls it with arguments from the stack. A crafted __reduce__ produces exactly that, so a shell command runs as soon as you load the file:

torch.load("model.bin", weights_only=False)
# same for pickle.load, joblib.load, np.load(..., allow_pickle=True)

PyTorch checkpoints are a zip with a pickle inside. joblib dumps are pickles. Object-dtype NumPy arrays store their data as a pickle. Recent PyTorch defaults to weights_only=True, but plenty of code and older installs still load full pickles. That is why pickle is the most common way a model file gets code execution.

How it reads a pickle without running it

pickle-model-scan walks the opcode stream with the standard library's pickletools.genops, which parses bytes and executes nothing. It records every import the stream would make and every call opcode, and reports:

  • a dangerous import (os, subprocess, builtins.eval, ...) together with REDUCE / BUILD / NEWOBJ: CRITICAL
  • deferred-call gadgets such as functools.partial or operator.attrgetter: HIGH
  • object-dtype NumPy arrays: HIGH
  • imports outside a known-safe allowlist of model reconstructors: MEDIUM, for review
  • zip entries that escape the extraction directory (Zip Slip): HIGH

It also tells you when a file is safetensors or GGUF, the formats with no code-execution surface.

The STACK_GLOBAL bypass

STACK_GLOBAL takes the module and name from the stack instead of from the opcode, so a scanner has to work out which strings were pushed before it. GHSA-9gvj-pp9x-gcfr (CVE-2025-71325, picklescan below 0.0.27) showed that picklescan and modelscan got this wrong. Their lookback skipped the string at position 0, so a crafted file could hide its os.system import and get past the scan. picklescan fixed it in 0.0.27.

pickle-model-scan uses the same "last two pushed strings" approach. On the advisory's own example it reports os.system with REDUCE as CRITICAL. When the operands can't be traced back to string literals (for example, they come from the memo or are built at load time), it doesn't stay quiet. It raises PKL007, "Unresolved STACK_GLOBAL operands", at HIGH. If it can't tell what an import is, it flags it instead of passing it.

Try it 

pip install "git+https://github.com/munimv2/keras-model-scan"

model-file-scan ./models                      # a file or a whole directory
model-file-scan pytorch_model.bin --json
model-file-scan ./models --sarif > model-file-scan.sarif
model-file-scan downloaded.pt --fail-on high || echo "do not load"

It uses only the standard library and needs Python 3.8+. Exit code 1 means there are findings at or above --fail-on. In CI, uses: munimv2/keras-model-scan@v0.3.0 uploads SARIF to the repository's Security tab.

Honest limits

  • It is a static heuristic, not a sandbox. A flag means "a person should look at this", not proof of malice, and a clean result is not a guarantee. If in doubt, don't load the file, and prefer safetensors.
  • Adversarial opcode reordering can still leave a file flagged as suspicious without the tool knowing what it imports.
  • lz4- and zstd-compressed containers are reported as unscanned. Decompress them first.

Please try it and open issues

If it gets a model file wrong (a false positive on a legitimate checkpoint, a bypass, or a format it misses), please open an issue: https://github.com/munimv2/keras-model-scan/issues. Bypasses are the most useful reports. Please don't attach live malicious files. Describe the opcode sequence instead.

title: Getting Started with the Gemini API: A Practical Tutorial
summary:
Getting Started with the Gemini API

The Gemini API lets you harness powerful language models for a variety of tasks—from generating text to analyzing data. This tutorial will walk you through setting up your environment, making your first request, and interpreting the response, all with a short, runnable Python example.

1. Prerequisites

  • Python 3.8+ installed on your machine.
  • requests library (pip install requests).
  • A Gemini API key from the Gemini console (you’ll need to create an account and enable the API).

2. Set Up the Request

Below is a minimal Python script that sends a prompt to the gemini-3.6-flash:free model and prints the generated text.

import requests
import json

API_KEY = "YOUR_API_KEY_HERE"
MODEL = "gemini-3.6-flash:free"
URL = f"https://api.unorouter.com/v1/chat/completions"

headers = {
    "Authorization": f"Bearer {API_KEY}",
    "Content-Type": "application/json"
}

payload = {
    "model": MODEL,
    "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Explain in two sentences what GPT-4 is."}],
    "stream": False
}

response = requests.post(URL, headers=headers, json=payload)
data = response.json()

if response.ok:
    # Extract the assistant's reply
    assistant_reply = data["choices"][0]["message"]["content"]
    print(assistant_reply)
else:
    print(f"Error: {data.get('error', 'Unknown error')}")

How It Works

  1. Headers – We authenticate with the API key and set the content type to JSON.
  2. Payload – The model field selects the free Gemini model. The messages array contains a single user message; you can adjust the prompt as needed.
  3. Response – On a successful request (200 OK), the generated text lives under choices[0].message.content.

3. Running the Script

Save the code to a file, e.g., gemini_demo.py, replace YOUR_API_KEY_HERE with your actual key, and run:

python gemini_demo.py

You should see a concise explanation of GPT‑4 printed to the console.

4. Tips & Best Practices

  • Rate Limits – The free tier includes a generous number of requests, but monitor your usage to avoid hitting limits.
  • Prompt Engineering – Clear, specific prompts yield more predictable results. Experiment with temperature settings if the API supports them.
  • Error Handling – Always check the response status and handle potential errors (e.g., network issues, invalid keys).

5. Next Steps

  • Explore other models (e.g., gemini-2.0-flash-exp) for different capabilities.
  • Integrate the API into larger applications using the official SDKs or REST calls.
  • Build simple tools like text summarizers, code assistants, or chatbots.

With just a few lines of code, you’ve unlocked the Gemini API’s potential. Happy coding!

title: Getting Started with the Gemini API
summary:
Getting Started with the Gemini API

The Gemini API is a powerful tool for developers to integrate AI capabilities into their applications. In this tutorial, we'll walk through the basics of using the Gemini API to generate text. The API is accessible via a simple HTTP endpoint and returns JSON responses.

Prerequisites

To get started, you'll need:

  • Python 3.6 or higher
  • The requests library (install with pip install requests)

Step 1: Get Your API Key

To use the Gemini API, you need an API key. You can obtain one by signing up at the Unorouter platform (or your preferred provider). Once you have your key, you can use it in your code. The key is a string that you include in the Authorization header of your requests.

Step 2: Write the API Request

Here's a simple Python example to call the Gemini API:

import requests

api_key = "YOUR_API_KEY"
url = "https://api.unorouter.com/v1/chat/completions"

payload = {
    "model": "gemini-3.6-flash:free",
    "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Hello, world!"}]
}

response = requests.post(url, json=payload, headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {api_key}"})

if response.status_code == 200:
    data = response.json()
    print(data["choices"][0]["message"]["content"])
else:
    print(f"Error: {response.status_code}")

This code sends a POST request to the API endpoint with a JSON payload. The model parameter specifies which model to use (in this case, the free Gemini model). The messages array contains the user's query.

Step 3: Interpret the Response

The response will be a JSON object. The choices array contains the generated text. The first element in the array (index 0) is the response from the model. The message object within the first choice contains the actual text.

Error Handling and Best Practices

When working with the API, it's important to handle errors gracefully. Common errors include:

  • Invalid API key (401 Unauthorized)
  • Invalid request (400 Bad Request)
  • Rate limiting (429 Too Many Requests)

Always check the response status code and handle errors appropriately. Also, consider using exponential backoff for rate-limited requests.

Conclusion

The Gemini API is straightforward to use and offers a free tier for development. With just a few lines of code, you can integrate AI into your applications. Start experimenting today!

The Gemini API is straightforward to use and offers a free tier for development. With just a few lines of code, you can integrate AI into your applications. Start experimenting today!

title: Before you read a codebase, draw its shape
summary:
Open a 300-file repo and the first thing you feel is vertigo. Which files are the project, and which are examples, assets, lockfiles, vendored junk? That ratio decides almost everything about how you read what follows, and most repos hide it.

So I wrote a small tool (shape.py, Python stdlib only) that prints a structural read of any folder in one screen: file count, total size, source size, the weight that isn't source, the top-level layout, and the largest source files.

Then I pointed it at repos I thought I already knew.

OpenAI's swarm is 6 files

The multi-agent framework everyone links. Here is the whole read:

shape  repos/swarm
  288 files   961.9k total   131.0k source
  entry points: pyproject.toml

  source languages
    python         131.0k   100%

  weight (not source)
    image 411.3k, config 394.5k, docs 24.4k, other 603B

  top level
    examples/    236 files   497.4k
    assets/        3 files   411.3k
    README.md      1 files    16.5k
    swarm/         6 files    16.1k
    tests/         5 files     9.3k
    logs/         31 files     7.7k

The framework itself, swarm/, is 6 files and 16 KB. The repo is 962 KB. The rest is examples/ (236 files) and assets/ (411 KB of images).

So when someone says "I read the swarm source," the honest part of that sentence is how little there was to read. The intimidating repo and the actual framework are two different sizes.

tqdm is one big file

A library most of us import without thinking. 97 files, 333 KB of source. The largest single file, tqdm/std.py, is 56.7 KB:

     56.7k  tqdm/std.py
     10.8k  tqdm/cli.py
     10.6k  tqdm/notebook.py
      9.6k  tqdm/contrib/concurrent.py

That's 17% of all source in one file. The thing you import to draw a progress bar is, structurally, one long file plus a thin perimeter.

Neither number is a judgement. std.py being large doesn't mean it's bad; a battle-tested progress bar has a lot of edge cases. The point is that this is knowable in about two seconds, and almost nobody knows it before they start.

Why "one screen"

The first question about unfamiliar code isn't "is it good." It's "where is the thing." A structure read answers that before you spend an afternoon in the wrong directory.

It's also the fastest way to catch a lie. I once had a repo whose docs directory was billed as a source module; the read showed 89% of "source" was misclassified, and I only saw it because I ran the tool on a repo I didn't write. Repeating that on strangers' repos is what fixed it.

What it isn't

It doesn't read semantics and it won't find your bug. It's a map, not a review. Treat a clean shape as "I know where to start," never "I know it's fine."

If you have a repo you've been avoiding because you can't tell where to start, I run these on request. Structural read, one screen, answered against whatever question you actually have about the codebase. Email me: katy-10@ilands.app

title: Focus Friend: An Executive Assistant Built for My Overwhelmed Friend Rahul
summary:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Weekend Challenge: Build for a Friend

What I Built

For my close friend rahul, opening Slack and email in the morning isn't just routine—it's an obstacle course of cognitive friction. rahul has ADHD, and when a 4-paragraph rambling email or a 15-person chaotic Slack thread lands in their inbox, Task Paralysis sets in. The brain gets overwhelmed trying to separate social fluff and emotional subtext from actual deliverables. The notification gets minimized, and the task gets forgotten.

Existing AI tools (like ChatGPT or Claude) often make this worse: they are conversational, chat-heavy, and require sending sensitive work emails to third-party cloud servers—a major privacy violation for work communications.

Focus Friend is a minimalist, local-first executive function companion built specifically to conquer this problem. It distills chaotic walls of text into three digestible data points in high-contrast Neo-Brutalist cards:

  1. 🔵 THE VIBE (Cyan Card): A one-sentence plain-English emotional temperature reading (e.g., "The boss is pleased with progress and only asks for a routine slide polish"). This immediately disarms rejection sensitivity and anxiety.
  2. 🔴 THE DEADLINE (Coral Card): Isolates the exact calendar date or delivery window from atmospheric fluff.
  3. 🟢 THE ACTION ITEM (Lime Card): A single, imperative-verb bullet point (e.g., "Review slide 7 metrics and reply with confirmation"). 1-click copy into Todoist or Slack so rahul can take action and close the app.

  • GitHub Repository: github.com/ezabhishek1/Focus-Friend (Anyone can test it instantly in their browser with the embedded Zero-Cloud Heuristic Engine and Overwhelm Presets, or run it locally connected to Microsoft Phi-3 via Ollama).

Dedicated to Alex ("The Overwhelmed Professional") and everyone navigating ADHD, neurodivergence, and cognitive overload in modern work environments.

Focus Friend is built with an unapologetic Neo-Brutalism UI Design System:

Open-weight models and open innovation matter profoundly for applications that interact with the physical world:

  1. Uncompromised Privacy for Living Spaces: Urban exploration starts right from where you live—your apartment block, dorm, or neighborhood street. Proprietary closed APIs demand that you pipe your daily geographic context, walking routines, and photos to third-party corporate servers. With open-weight models, 0 bytes of personal habit data leave your device.
  2. Offline Resilience on Trails & Alleys: Real-world walks often take you into city parks, subway underpasses, or trail segments with poor cellular coverage. Closed API apps immediately fail when connection drops; open models running locally continue functioning in airplane mode.
  3. No Metered Billing Anxiety: Overcoming burnout shouldn't come with token quotas or surprise API bills. Open models empower builders to deliver free, resilient community utilities that anyone can run forever.

title: Code Search RAG: Chunk by Function With tree-sitter, Not by 512 Tokens
summary:
• Book: RAG Pocket Guide
  • Also by me: Thinking in Go (2-book series) — Complete Guide to Go Programming + Hexagonal Architecture in Go
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

The chunk the codebase assistant retrieved for "where does the retry delay get computed?" starts halfway down a function, at an except clause, and has no def line, no class name, nothing but a file path to say where it came from. The model writes a confident answer about a function it never saw the name of.

The bug is in the chunker. It cut the file every 512 tokens, the way it cuts prose, and the cut landed in the middle of a function. Code has natural seams at def and class; a token counter ignores them.

The fix fits in two small files. Parse Python with tree-sitter, cut at function and class boundaries, carry the file path and the enclosing symbol as metadata, and split the definitions that are too big on statement boundaries. Then score both chunkers on a labelled query set, so you see the difference on your own machine instead of taking my word for it.

What a token window does to a function

A fixed window has no idea where a function starts. If a function begins at token 470 of a 512-token window, the chunk gets the decorator, the signature and four lines of body. The next chunk gets the rest of the body with no name attached. Ask for "the function that parses the config file" and the retriever has to match either a signature with no logic or logic with no signature.

The cAST paper from Carnegie Mellon and Augment Code found the same problem: "Existing line-based chunking heuristics often break semantic structures, splitting functions or merging unrelated code." Their AST-based chunker, which splits large syntax nodes and merges small siblings under a size limit, reported a 4.3-point Recall@5 gain on RepoEval retrieval and a 2.67-point Pass@1 gain on SWE-bench generation over the fixed-size baseline.

Frameworks have moved the same way. LlamaIndex ships a CodeSplitter that parses with tree-sitter and, in its source, caps chunks at 1,500 characters by default. The cAST authors published astchunk, which measures chunk size in non-whitespace characters and supports Python, Java, C# and TypeScript. Both are fine to use. Writing your own once is how you find out what they are doing for you, and how you tune it when your codebase has 600-line functions.


Token windows cut wherever the count runs out. AST chunks cut where the code does.

Two chunkers, same token budget

Install the pieces. py-tree-sitter 0.26.0 needs Python 3.10 or newer, and the Python grammar ships as its own wheel.

pip install tree-sitter tree-sitter-python \
  sentence-transformers numpy

The embedder is BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5: a small English model with 384 dimensions and a 512-token max sequence length. Both chunkers get the same budget of 480 tokens, counted with the embedder's own tokenizer, so a short header and the special tokens still fit under 512 and nothing gets silently truncated. That is the fair version of "512-token chunks".

First file, chunkers.py, starting with the Chunk type:

# chunkers.py
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Callable

import tree_sitter_python as tspython
from tree_sitter import Language, Parser

PARSER = Parser(Language(tspython.language()))
DEFS = {"function_definition", "class_definition"}
Count = Callable[[str], int]

@dataclass
class Chunk:
    path: str
    symbol: str  # "JSONDecoder.raw_decode", "", or ""
    start: int   # 1-based first line
    end: int     # 1-based last line, inclusive
    text: str

    def embed_text(self) -> str:
        head = f"# {self.path}"
        if self.symbol:
            head += f" :: {self.symbol}"
        return f"{head}\n{self.text}"

The baseline comes next. It adds lines while their token count stays under the budget, emits a chunk, then backs up about 64 tokens for the overlap. The BGE tokenizer emits no token for a newline, so summing per line counts the same tokens the AST chunker counts on joined text:

# chunkers.py (continued)
def fixed_chunks(path: str, src: str, ntok: Count,
                 size: int = 480, overlap: int = 64):
    lines = src.split("\n")
    out, i = [], 0
    while i < len(lines):
        j, used = i, 0
        while j < len(lines):
            cost = ntok(lines[j])
            if used + cost > size and j > i:
                break
            used += cost
            j += 1
        text = "\n".join(lines[i:j])
        out.append(Chunk(path, "", i + 1, j, text))
        if j >= len(lines):
            break
        back, k = 0, j
        while k > i + 1 and back < overlap:
            k -= 1
            back += ntok(lines[k])
        i = k
    return out

The baseline is slightly generous: it snaps to line ends and overlaps about 64 tokens, where a plain token splitter would cut mid-line. Its chunks still get the file path in the header. The only things it lacks are syntax-aware boundaries and the symbol name, which keeps the comparison about exactly those two things.

src.split("\n") rather than splitlines() is deliberate. tree-sitter counts rows by \n only, and splitlines() also splits on form feeds, which some older Python files contain. Mixing the two puts every line number after the first form feed off by one.

The AST chunker goes in the same file. First the helpers that write chunks:

# chunkers.py (continued)
def unwrap(node):
    if node.type == "decorated_definition":
        return node.child_by_field_name("definition")
    return node

def name_of(defn) -> str:
    return defn.child_by_field_name("name").text.decode()

def ast_chunks(path: str, src: str, ntok: Count,
               budget: int = 480):
    lines = src.split("\n")
    tree = PARSER.parse(src.encode())
    out: list[Chunk] = []

    def span(a, b):  # 0-based rows, inclusive
        return "\n".join(lines[a:b + 1])

    def emit(sym, a, b, head=""):
        body = span(a, b)
        if ntok(head + body) <= budget:
            out.append(Chunk(path, sym, a + 1, b + 1, head + body))
            return
        # one statement is bigger than the budget: window it
        room = max(budget - ntok(head), 64)
        for c in fixed_chunks(path, body, ntok, size=room):
            out.append(Chunk(path, sym, a + c.start, a + c.end,
                             head + c.text))

emit writes one chunk when the span fits and falls back to line windows only when a single statement is bigger than the budget. pack sits on top of it and greedily groups neighbouring statements. It is still inside ast_chunks, so keep the indentation:

    # ast_chunks, continued
    def pack(nodes, sym, head=""):
        group = []
        for node in nodes:
            if group:
                a = group[0].start_point[0]
                b = node.end_point[0]
                if ntok(head + span(a, b)) > budget:
                    emit(sym, a, group[-1].end_point[0], head)
                    group = []
            group.append(node)
        if group:
            emit(sym, group[0].start_point[0],
                 group[-1].end_point[0], head)

The last two helpers decide what a unit is, and the final line starts the walk at the module root:

    # ast_chunks, continued
    def define(node, defn, scope):
        name = name_of(defn)
        sym = f"{scope}.{name}" if scope else name
        a, b = node.start_point[0], node.end_point[0]
        if ntok(span(a, b)) <= budget:
            emit(sym, a, b)
            return
        body = defn.child_by_field_name("body")
        head = span(a, body.start_point[0] - 1) + "\n"
        if defn.type == "class_definition":
            block(body.named_children, sym, head)
        else:
            pack(body.named_children, sym, head)

    def block(nodes, scope, head=""):
        loose = []
        for node in nodes:
            defn = unwrap(node)
            if defn.type in DEFS:
                if loose:
                    pack(loose, scope or "", head)
                    loose = []
                define(node, defn, scope)
            else:
                loose.append(node)
        if loose:
            pack(loose, scope or "", head)

    block(tree.root_node.named_children, "")
    return out

Walk it top-down. block goes through the statements of a module or a class body. Each definition goes to define, and the statements between definitions (imports, constants, a class docstring) collect into loose and get packed into chunks or chunks named after the class. define emits a definition whole if it fits. Decorators count as part of the definition, because tree-sitter-python wraps them in a decorated_definition whose definition field holds the function or class.

The symbol path is the breadcrumb. A method inside JSONDecoder gets JSONDecoder.raw_decode, and embed_text() puts # json/decoder.py :: JSONDecoder.raw_decode on the first line of what gets embedded. A query that says "JSON decoder" now has a literal match even when the method body never says it.

When one function is bigger than the budget

Function-level chunks break down on the big ones. A 300-line class or a 200-line function does not fit in 480 tokens, and dumping it whole into the embedder does not help. The model card for all-MiniLM-L6-v2 says so directly: "By default, input text longer than 256 word pieces is truncated." Everything past the cutoff is invisible to retrieval, and nothing warns you.

The chunker above handles size in three steps.

What I Built

I built Local Seller AI, an AI-powered marketing copilot for small business owners, local shopkeepers, and side hustlers.

It helps sellers create product descriptions, social media captions, WhatsApp promotional messages, and SEO keywords. It also includes a pricing calculator and a 7-day marketing planner.

Small sellers often have limited time and budget for marketing. This tool brings these tasks together in one simple app, helping them save time and organize their business activities.

It is designed for local shopkeepers, home-based businesses, and freelancers who want an affordable way to manage everyday marketing tasks.

title: Quality video on local hardware: the Elsewhere Unfolds workflow
summary:
Local models can produce beautiful shots. A finished film needs more: a world that stays coherent, movement that feels intentional, music that holds together, and an edit worth watching. This is the production method we have been developing with Elsewhere Unfolds.

An early Elsewhere Unfolds cut had an attractive world, a complete timeline, and a successful render. It also had water that barely moved and clouds that stayed fixed while the camera drifted past them.

The shot manifest was satisfied. The scene did not feel alive.

That correction changed how we produced the next passages. We separated camera movement from environmental movement, tested short motion clips at normal speed, and watched them before committing to the rest of the film. The improvement came from a clearer creative requirement and a smaller review loop.

Elsewhere Unfolds makes fantasy and cosmic visual journeys with instrumental music. This guide explains the reusable production method behind that work, from the first visual promise to a finished master and vertical excerpts.

The boundary matters: our established motion, music, editing, and finishing pipeline uses local resources. Some starting images were made with a hosted image tool. That makes those productions hybrid. For an entirely local version, supply your own photographs, drawings, local 3D renders, or images from a model running on your machine. The workflow below starts with those local image files. It does not require a hosted video generator.

The examples use the Wan 2.2 TI2V-5B and ACE-Step v1 stack from our production recipes. They are a concrete baseline, not a claim that every newer model has been evaluated or that these settings suit every GPU.

The production loop

Work in three sizes: one shot, one short sequence, then the complete film. Each answers a different question.

Size What you are learning What to review
One native motion take Can the intended action work? Geometry, feet, motion direction, unwanted objects
A 30 to 60 second sequence Do the shots and music belong together? Orientation, pacing, transitions, emotional tone
The complete film Does the experience hold up over time? Repetition, later continuity, score joins, ending

Our longer episodes have used an 8:01 format. That is an editorial choice, not a recommended starting assignment. Begin with a 30-second film you can finish, inspect, and revise. Padding a weak minute into eight minutes only gives you more weak material to fix.

What needs to run locally

You do not need a cluster. You need a machine that can run the chosen model, space for its weights and intermediate files, and a way to edit and review the result.

Job Our established tool or method Output to keep
World and shot planning Written brief, storyboard, reference images Selected brief and shot list
Starting artwork Approved image files; source can vary Original plate and provenance
Image-to-video motion Wan 2.2 TI2V-5B Native take, prompt, seed, settings
Instrumental music ACE-Step v1 3.5B Raw WAVs and selected arrangement
Assembly and finishing Python orchestration and FFmpeg Edit decisions, review copy, final master
Inspection FFprobe, frame samples, normal playback Technical results and review decisions

Wan's documented single-GPU TI2V-5B example targets at least 24 GB of VRAM with model offloading and the text encoder on CPU. Treat that as the reference for that command, not a universal minimum or a guarantee of success. CPU RAM, free VRAM, software versions, and the selected settings still matter. Check the official Wan setup instructions against your hardware before downloading a large checkpoint.

For a first project, keep motion generation and music generation sequential. A background model can consume memory that a video job needs. If the GPU is shared, agree on an available window; do not terminate somebody else's work to make room. A waiting job is cheaper than losing an accepted take or disrupting another workload.

Initial installation and model downloads need network access. Local inference means the generation runs on your equipment. It does not make electricity, storage, setup time, or retakes free.

Record the model revision, source revision, environment, settings, and input image for each run. A seed helps repeat an experiment, but it does not guarantee identical output across different software and hardware.

1. Write the experience before writing prompts

A useful brief explains what the viewer will experience and what will change. “Beautiful cinematic fantasy, ultra detailed” cannot do that work.

Here is an illustrative brief for a small film:

We board a floating garden before it leaves a quiet dock. A gardener crosses the terrace. The gap behind us widens, and a pale arch appears at our destination. Copper, emerald, and pearl remain the visual palette. The mood is calm anticipation. The final image resolves the journey rather than introducing another location.

Turn it into a few fixed decisions:

  • The promise: a garden really leaves one place for another.
  • The route: boarding terrace, departure view, onboard path, destination.
  • The continuity anchors: the same moon placement, architecture, clothing, and direction of travel.
  • The movement: leaves and water move; the dock recedes; a person performs one readable action.
  • The exclusions: no crowds, complicated hand exchanges, or unexplained new landmarks.

Make the thumbnail and first shot agree about the film's promise. If the packaging promises a moving island, establish that island and its departure early. A long logo introduction spends attention before delivering the thing the viewer selected.

For Elsewhere, a recognizable route matters more than a collection of unrelated beautiful locations. Each shot should tell us where we are, what has changed, or where we are going.

2. Build a world that survives the next camera angle

Call the approved starting image for a shot its plate. Keep a small set of reference plates that establish materials, light, landmarks, and any recurring people.

Review the plates together before animating them. A contact sheet makes inconsistencies easier to see: a second moon appears, the destination moves behind the traveler, or a bridge no longer connects to the same terrace.

We have caught all of those classes of problem during production. One reverse view placed another complete moon outside a doorway even though the camera was already inside that moon. Another reference combination duplicated the sun. Attractive individual images can still describe an impossible route.

Use a compact shot table:

Shot Purpose Action Must remain stable
Terrace wide Establish the world Water ripples and leaves move Island silhouette, moon position
Gardener profile Establish habitation One walk from left to right Clothing, ground contact, path
Stern view Prove departure The distant dock recedes Foreground rail, open gap
Bow view Reveal destination Gentle camera reveal Travel direction, destination arch

Simplify a plate when it asks too much of motion generation. Give a walking person visible feet, clear ground, and empty space ahead. Separate actions that would otherwise compete. A close hand exchange, turning crowd, and moving camera in the same five seconds create several opportunities for failure.

If you want the whole process to stay local, this is where you choose your image source. A scene rendered in a local 3D application or a drawing you made yourself is a valid plate. A local image model is another option, but it is a separate tool to qualify. We are not claiming that substituting one reproduces our hosted artwork automatically.

3. Generate one motion take with a clear job

For image-to-video work, let the plate describe the appearance. Use the motion prompt to describe the action, camera, and things that must stay stable.

An illustrative prompt:

Locked medium-wide side view. One gardener walks naturally from left to right along the level stone path. Both feet remain visible and contact the ground. Leaves move gently in the background. Preserve the copper railing, architecture, clothing, and lighting. No additional people, no camera orbit, no cuts.

After following the upstream installation instructions and downloading the TI2V-5B checkpoint, this is the shape of a run from the Wan source directory. Replace the example input and checkpoint paths with your local files. Use a new output filename for each attempt.

python generate.py \
  --task ti2v-5B \
  --size '1280*704' \
  --ckpt_dir ./Wan2.2-TI2V-5B \
  --image ./inputs/gardener.png \
  --prompt 'Locked side view. One gardener walks left to right on a level path. Feet remain visible. Leaves move gently. Preserve the railing and clothing. No extra people or cuts.' \
  --frame_num 121 \
  --sample_steps 50 \
  --sample_solver unipc \
  --sample_shift 5.0 \
  --sample_guide_scale 5.0 \
  --base_seed 42 \
  --offload_model True \
  --convert_model_dtype \
  --t5_cpu \
  --save_file ./gardener-take-01.mp4

These controls follow the upstream command-line interface and our established recipe. This is an adapted example, not a fresh performance benchmark. It does not enable a hosted prompt-expansion service.

At 24 fps, 121 encoded frames occupy about 5.04 seconds. An exact five-second edit uses 120 frames. Check the generated file's actual dimensions and timing: our image-conditioned production outputs have included 1248 × 704, despite the 1280*704 size setting. Do not infer the output raster from the command alone.

Watch the native take before slowing, enlarging, or stitching it. Check the start, middle, and end, then play the entire clip. Look for foot sliding, changing faces, bending rails, sudden foreground figures, and movement in the wrong direction. If the action fails, simplify the action or repair the plate before launching a large batch.

4. Treat three kinds of motion separately

Camera motion changes the viewpoint. Environmental motion changes water, mist, foliage, light, and other scene elements. Performed action is a person walking, turning, or doing something.

An image can have a convincing camera move while its waterfall remains frozen. A scene can have moving fog while its traveler slides without taking a step. Review each kind independently.

For a calm environmental shot, forward slow motion can be useful if it still looks natural. For walking or other recognizable human actions, start with native speed. Watch any interpolation for doubled limbs, smeared edges, and unstable occlusions.

Five seconds of generated movement do not become twenty seconds of new action because the editor can repeat or slow them. A reverse loop can make a person walk backward; a repeated wave or bird can reveal the loop. If a passage needs more time, generate a distinct take, cut to another angle, or shorten the passage.

Continuing from the last frame of a previous take can help connect movement, but it can also carry defects forward. Inspect that frame before making it the next input. Stop a continuation when geometry starts to drift instead of extending the error through the film.

5. Finish a short opening before expanding the film

Assemble a 30 to 60 second proof with real motion, representative music, and the intended edit rhythm. A slideshow of selected plates cannot answer whether the finished motion works.

The proof should contain the hard part. If departure is the central promise, include departure. If a recurring traveler makes the world feel inhabited, include a real walking shot. An easy landscape does not qualify a harder action later.

Review the sequence without pausing first. Does it make sense? Does the first shot deliver the promise? Is there a reason to keep watching? Then examine technical defects and individual transitions.

Once a sequence is accepted, keep its exact files and settings. Expand around it. We preserve accepted openings while generating later passages so a new render cannot silently replace the part that already worked.

Keep a simple project layout:

film/
  brief.md
  shots.csv
  plates/
  motion/raw/
  motion/selected/
  music/raw/
  music/selected/
  edit/
  review/
  exports/

The labels are less important than the separation. Raw sources stay intact; selected sources are explicit; review exports are disposable derivatives. Save a rejection reason beside a failed take so the next attempt changes something useful.

6. Compose and review the soundtrack as a whole

Our established music recipes use ACE-Step v1 3.5B locally. Keep the version explicit: a later release may have different installation, controls, and behavior. Use the project's documentation for the environment matching your selected release.

A music brief should describe the experience and the arrangement. For this style, we ask for warm, spacious instrumental ambience, gradual harmony, and sparse melody. We also describe what would break the mood: lyrics, voice-like passages, a strong beat, abrupt motifs, or a trailer-style crescendo.

Start with a short audition against the opening. Choose where the cue enters and whether it leaves enough space for the imagery. Then review the full arrangement, including every join and the final tail. An attractive first minute does not establish a clean ending.

Keep lossless WAV sources. Build an arrangement from selected cues with measured overlaps, deliberate fades, and enough headroom. The finished duration is the sum of the cue durations minus their overlaps. The same arithmetic applies to overlapping video transitions.

Measure the generated audio rather than assuming a requested duration is exact. We encountered a cue that was roughly 73 milliseconds short because of the installed model's duration grid. The composition had succeeded. The useful response was to preserve it, diagnose the precise discrepancy, and make a small documented finishing correction. That is different from concealing a missing passage with silence.

Check the playback path before removing noise

When static is reported, compare the original WAV, the finished export, and playback in another native player or device. In one later Elsewhere review, native Windows playback sounded correct while the WSL playback path did not. Filtering the accepted source would have changed music that was already satisfactory.

For a different batch of Shorts, a gentle cleanup was accepted after direct comparison. This was the filter used for that case:

ffmpeg -n -i source.wav \
  -af 'afftdn=nr=6:nf=-48:tn=0:gs=8' \
  -c:a pcm_s24le audition-clean.wav

Treat this as an audition candidate, never an automatic mastering preset. FFmpeg documents these controls under afftdn. Denoising can soften wanted texture. Compare original and cleaned versions at comparable listening levels, preserve both, and choose by listening. Waveform similarity and successful decoding cannot establish that something sounds good.

7. Edit to a timeline, not a requested runtime

Give every shot an editorial purpose and an explicit frame allocation. At 24 fps, an 8:01 film contains 11,544 presentation frames. Resolve transitions and overlaps in that frame budget rather than rounding each shot independently.

For a first 30-second exercise, prepare six accepted five-second shots at 24 fps, all with matching dimensions, codec settings, and no audio. Put the filenames in edit/shots.txt, relative to that list:

file '../motion/selected/shot-01.mp4'
file '../motion/selected/shot-02.mp4'
file '../motion/selected/shot-03.mp4'
file '../motion/selected/shot-04.mp4'
file '../motion/selected/shot-05.mp4'
file '../motion/selected/shot-06.mp4'

From the project root, assemble a straight-cut picture track:

ffmpeg -n -f concat -safe 0 -i edit/shots.txt \
  -map 0:v:0 -an -c:v copy edit/picture.mp4

This simple stream-copy path requires compatible, independently prepared clips. Mixed time bases, encoders, or track layouts need normalization in your editing stage; a concat command is not a general repair tool. Keep crossfades out of the first exercise so its duration stays easy to audit. See the concat demuxer documentation.

After preparing a 30-second score with its entrance and ending already shaped, make a review export:

ffmpeg -n -i edit/picture.mp4 -i music/selected/score-30s.wav \
  -map 0:v:0 -map 1:a:0 \
  -c:v copy -c:a aac -b:a 320k -ar 48000 \
  -movflags +faststart exports/review-30s.mp4

Both sources must cover the intended duration. Avoid adding -shortest as a reflex: it can hide an unexpectedly short input by cutting the other track. Inspect the result and listen to its ending.

Keep the native generation size distinct from the delivery size. A 3840 × 2160 export made from lower-resolution motion is an upscale. It can be a useful delivery format, but enlarging a warped railing makes a larger warped railing. Finish motion and continuity before paying for a high-resolution encode.

8. Make quality control answer specific questions

Automated checks are useful when they tell you exactly what they established. Use FFprobe to inspect the exported file:

ffprobe -v error -count_frames \
  -show_entries 'stream=index,codec_type,codec_name,width,height,avg_frame_rate,nb_read_frames,duration,sample_rate,channels:format=duration' \
  -of json exports/review-30s.mp4

For the exercise, expect 720 video frames at 24 fps and the planned audio channels and sample rate. AAC/container timing can differ slightly from the exact picture duration; investigate meaningful mismatches instead of treating every reported duration as identical.

Decode the entire export, including audio:

ffmpeg -v error -xerror -i exports/review-30s.mp4 \
  -map 0:v:0 -map 0:a:0 -f null -

A clean decode establishes readable media. It does not establish pleasing images, good pacing, or acceptable sound. Complete three reviews:

Review Questions
Technical Does it decode? Are the streams, dimensions, frame count, and duration correct?
Visual Does the world stay coherent? Do feet, rails, water, and transitions behave?
Listening Are cue joins, noise, dynamics, and the ending acceptable on real playback?

Sample frames around transitions and at the middle of procedural effects, not just the first and last frames. We caught a highlight problem at the peak of a light treatment: an 8-bit color calculation exceeded its valid range and wrapped. The endpoints looked fine. The fix was in the finishing calculation, not another generation attempt.

When replacing one part of an accepted film, verify that the parts meant to stay unchanged did stay unchanged. File hashes identify exact copies. Decoded-frame comparisons can check preserved picture across a container change. Neither substitutes for watching the new result.

9. Expand, recover, and keep the good work

A long render has more than one kind of success. Generation can finish even if a later copy, collection, or resource-restoration step fails. Inspect the output before rerunning the expensive part.

Save completed takes as they arrive. Record the input plate, prompt, seed, model revision, native output, and selected derivative for each shot. If a job is interrupted, resume from the missing work instead of regenerating everything that already passed review.

On shared hardware, record what resource settings you changed and restore those settings after the run. Check that restoration separately from the video artifact. A good clip does not prove the machine was returned to its previous state.

Agents and scripts are helpful for preparing shot packets, tracking outputs, making contact sheets, checking files, and assembling review pages. Give them explicit limits on retries, durations, and replacement scope. Keep creative selection with the person watching and listening. A process reporting success cannot decide that a walk feels natural.

The useful efficiency measure is accepted footage per production session. A faster model that creates more unusable takes may cost more time overall. Track rejected takes and the reasons for rejection before changing models or increasing concurrency.

10. Derive Shorts from the accepted film

Choose excerpts that contain a complete visual idea: a reveal, an arrival, a short action, or a change in the world. Reframe deliberately for vertical output. A centered crop can remove the destination, the feet, or the object that makes the action understandable.

Elsewhere's vertical edits reuse the accepted picture and soundtrack. Review the new crop, text placement, entrance, and ending as a separate edit. Keep a clean version as well as any version carrying a short hook or invitation to the full film. Captions belong where there is speech or useful context; an instrumental film does not need invented narration.

Watch the export at phone size with the platform's interface area in mind. Keep the important action visible, and listen to the actual exported audio. A short excerpt can expose a rough music boundary that was unnoticeable inside a longer cue.

Publication adds another review: correct file, title, thumbnail, links, visibility, processing, and playback. Follow the platform's current disclosure requirements. Local generation and an original prompt do not settle every source or usage question; retain the provenance and applicable licenses for the material you use.

Measure the audience response separately from production quality. Compare retention and traffic sources at similar release ages where possible. A Short's views do not prove that viewers continued to the full film, and a small audience sample does not establish why one opening performed differently.

Your first local film

Make the first deliverable small enough to finish:

  1. Write one paragraph describing a place, an action, and an ending.
  2. Select a small set of locally sourced plates that agree about the world.
  3. Prove the hardest action in one native motion take.
  4. Build six distinct five-second shots with consistent technical settings.
  5. Select or compose a local 30-second soundtrack and shape its ending.
  6. Assemble, probe, decode, watch, and listen to the complete export.
  7. Preserve the accepted version before trying a longer film or a vertical cut.

The lasting part of the Elsewhere workflow is the ability to inspect and revise each decision. You can replace a model, change an editor, or improve the hardware while keeping that method: define the experience, test its hardest part, preserve what works, and judge the film that the viewer will actually see.

A local image model is another option, but it is a separate tool to qualify. We are not claiming that substituting one reproduces our hosted artwork automatically.

3. Generate one motion take with a clear job

For image-to-video work, let the plate describe the appearance. Use the motion prompt to describe the action, camera, and things that must stay stable.

An illustrative prompt:

Locked medium-wide side view. One gardener walks naturally from left to right along the level stone path. Both feet remain visible and contact the ground. Leaves move gently in the background. Preserve the copper railing, architecture, clothing, and lighting. No additional people, no camera orbit, no cuts.

After following the upstream installation instructions and downloading the TI2V-5B checkpoint, this is the shape of a run from the Wan source directory. Replace the example input and checkpoint paths with your local files. Use a new output filename for each attempt.

python generate.py \
  --task ti2v-5B \
  --size '1280*704' \
  --ckpt_dir ./Wan2.2-TI2V-5B \
  --image ./inputs/gardener.png \
  --prompt 'Locked side view. One gardener walks left to right on a level path. Feet remain visible. Leaves move gently. Preserve the railing and clothing. No extra people or cuts.' \
  --frame_num 121 \
  --sample_steps 50 \
  --sample_solver unipc \
  --sample_shift 5.0 \
  --sample_guide_scale 5.0 \
  --base_seed 42 \
  --offload_model True \
  --convert_model_dtype \
  --t5_cpu \
  --save_file ./gardener-take-01.mp4

These controls follow the upstream command-line interface and our established recipe. This is an adapted example, not a fresh performance benchmark. It does not enable a hosted prompt-expansion service.

At 24 fps, 121 encoded frames occupy about 5.04 seconds. An exact five-second edit uses 120 frames. Check the generated file's actual dimensions and timing: our image-conditioned production outputs have included 1248 × 704, despite the 1280*704 size setting. Do not infer the output raster from the command alone.

Watch the native take before slowing, enlarging, or stitching it. Check the start, middle, and end, then play the entire clip. Look for foot sliding, changing faces, bending rails, sudden foreground figures, and movement in the wrong direction. If the action fails, simplify the action or repair the plate before launching a large batch.

4. Treat three kinds of motion separately

Camera motion changes the viewpoint. Environmental motion changes water, mist, foliage, light, and other scene elements. Performed action is a person walking, turning, or doing something.

An image can have a convincing camera move while its waterfall remains frozen. A scene can have moving fog while its traveler slides without taking a step. Review each kind independently.

For a calm environmental shot, forward slow motion can be useful if it still looks natural. For walking or other recognizable human actions, start with native speed. Watch any interpolation for doubled limbs, smeared edges, and unstable occlusions.

Five seconds of generated movement do not become twenty seconds of new action because the editor can repeat or slow them. A reverse loop can make a person walk backward; a repeated wave or bird can reveal the loop. If a passage needs more time, generate a distinct take, cut to another angle, or shorten the passage.

Continuing from the last frame of a previous take can help connect movement, but it can also carry defects forward. Inspect that frame before making it the next input. Stop a continuation when geometry starts to drift instead of extending the error through the film.

5. Finish a short opening before expanding the film

Assemble a 30 to 60 second proof with real motion, representative music, and the intended edit rhythm. A slideshow of selected plates cannot answer whether the finished motion works.

The proof should contain the hard part. If departure is the central promise, include departure. If a recurring traveler makes the world feel inhabited, include a real walking shot. An easy landscape does not qualify a harder action later.

Review the sequence without pausing first. Does it make sense? Does the first shot deliver the promise? Is there a reason to keep watching? Then examine technical defects and individual transitions.

Once a sequence is accepted, keep its exact files and settings. Expand around it. We preserve accepted openings while generating later passages so a new render cannot silently replace the part that already worked.

Keep a simple project layout:

film/
  brief.md
  shots.csv
  plates/
  motion/raw/
  motion/selected/
  music/raw/
  music/selected/
  edit/
  review/
  exports/

The labels are less important than the separation. Raw sources stay intact; selected sources are explicit; review exports are disposable derivatives. Save a rejection reason beside a failed take so the next attempt changes something useful.

6. Compose and review the soundtrack as a whole

Our established music recipes use ACE-Step v1 3.5B locally. Keep the version explicit: a later release may have different installation, controls, and behavior. Use the project's documentation for the environment matching your selected release.

A music brief should describe the experience and the arrangement. For this style, we ask for warm, spacious instrumental ambience, gradual harmony, and sparse melody. We also describe what would break the mood: lyrics, voice-like passages, a strong beat, abrupt motifs, or a trailer-style crescendo.

Start with a short audition against the opening. Choose where the cue enters and whether it leaves enough space for the imagery. Then review the full arrangement, including every join and the final tail. An attractive first minute does not establish a clean ending.

Keep lossless WAV sources. Build an arrangement from selected cues with measured overlaps, deliberate fades, and enough headroom. The finished duration is the sum of the cue durations minus their overlaps. The same arithmetic applies to overlapping video transitions.

Measure the generated audio rather than assuming a requested duration is exact. We encountered a cue that was roughly 73 milliseconds short because of the installed model's duration grid. The composition had succeeded. The useful response was to preserve it, diagnose the precise discrepancy, and make a small documented finishing correction. That is different from concealing a missing passage with silence.

Check the playback path before removing noise

When static is reported, compare the original WAV, the finished export, and playback in another native player or device. In one later Elsewhere review, native Windows playback sounded correct while the WSL playback path did not. Filtering the accepted source would have changed music that was already satisfactory.

For a different batch of Shorts, a gentle cleanup was accepted after direct comparison. This was the filter used for that case:

ffmpeg -n -i source.wav \
  -af 'afftdn=nr=6:nf=-48:tn=0:gs=8' \
  -c:a pcm_s24le audition-clean.wav

Treat this as an audition candidate, never an automatic mastering preset. FFmpeg documents these controls under afftdn. Denoising can soften wanted texture. Compare original and cleaned versions at comparable listening levels, preserve both, and choose by listening. Waveform similarity and successful decoding cannot establish that something sounds good.

7. Edit to a timeline, not a requested runtime

Give every shot an editorial purpose and an explicit frame allocation. At 24 fps, an 8:01 film contains 11,544 presentation frames. Resolve transitions and overlaps in that frame budget rather than rounding each shot independently.

For a first 30-second exercise, prepare six accepted five-second shots at 24 fps, all with matching dimensions, codec settings, and no audio. Put the filenames in edit/shots.txt, relative to that list:

file '../motion/selected/shot-01.mp4'
file '../motion/selected/shot-02.mp4'
file '../motion/selected/shot-03.mp4'
file '../motion/selected/shot-04.mp4'
file '../motion/selected/shot-05.mp4'
file '../motion/selected/shot-06.mp4'

From the project root, assemble a straight-cut picture track:

ffmpeg -n -f concat -safe 0 -i edit/shots.txt \
  -map 0:v:0 -an -c:v copy edit/picture.mp4

This simple stream-copy path requires compatible, independently prepared clips. Mixed time bases, encoders, or track layouts need normalization in your editing stage; a concat command is not a general repair tool. Keep crossfades out of the first exercise so its duration stays easy to audit. See the concat demuxer documentation.

After preparing a 30-second score with its entrance and ending already shaped, make a review export:

ffmpeg -n -i edit/picture.mp4 -i music/selected/score-30s.wav \
  -map 0:v:0 -map 1:a:0 \
  -c:v copy -c:a aac -b:a 320k -ar 48000 \
  -movflags +faststart exports/review-30s.mp4

Both sources must cover the intended duration. Avoid adding -shortest as a reflex: it can hide an unexpectedly short input by cutting the other track. Inspect the result and listen to its ending.

Keep the native generation size distinct from the delivery size. A 3840 × 2160 export made from lower-resolution motion is an upscale. It can be a useful delivery format, but enlarging a warped railing makes a larger warped railing. Finish motion and continuity before paying for a high-resolution encode.

8. Make quality control answer specific questions

Automated checks are useful when they tell you exactly what they established. Use FFprobe to inspect the exported file:

ffprobe -v error -count_frames \
  -show_entries 'stream=index,codec_type,codec_name,width,height,avg_frame_rate,nb_read_frames,duration,sample_rate,channels:format=duration' \
  -of json exports/review-30s.mp4

For the exercise, expect 720 video frames at 24 fps and the planned audio channels and sample rate. AAC/container timing can differ slightly from the exact picture duration; investigate meaningful mismatches instead of treating every reported duration as identical.

Decode the entire export, including audio:

ffmpeg -v error -xerror -i exports/review-30s.mp4 \
  -map 0:v:0 -map 0:a:0 -f null -

A clean decode establishes readable media. It does not establish pleasing images, good pacing, or acceptable sound. Complete three reviews:

Review Questions
Technical Does it decode? Are the streams, dimensions, frame count, and duration correct?
Visual Does the world stay coherent? Do feet, rails, water, and transitions behave?
Listening Are cue joins, noise, dynamics, and the ending acceptable on real playback?

Sample frames around transitions and at the middle of procedural effects, not just the first and last frames. We caught a highlight problem at the peak of a light treatment: an 8-bit color calculation exceeded its valid range and wrapped. The endpoints looked fine. The fix was in the finishing calculation, not another generation attempt.

When replacing one part of an accepted film, verify that the parts meant to stay unchanged did stay unchanged. File hashes identify exact copies. Decoded-frame comparisons can check preserved picture across a container change. Neither substitutes for watching the new result.

9. Expand, recover, and keep the good work

A long render has more than one kind of success. Generation can finish even if a later copy, collection, or resource-restoration step fails. Inspect the output before rerunning the expensive part.

Save completed takes as they arrive. Record the input plate, prompt, seed, model revision, native output, and selected derivative for each shot. If a job is interrupted, resume from the missing work instead of regenerating everything that already passed review.

On shared hardware, record what resource settings you changed and restore those settings after the run. Check that restoration separately from the video artifact. A good clip does not prove the machine was returned to its previous state.

Agents and scripts are helpful for preparing shot packets, tracking outputs, making contact sheets, checking files, and assembling review pages. Give them explicit limits on retries, durations, and replacement scope. Keep creative selection with the person watching and listening. A process reporting success cannot decide that a walk feels natural.

The useful efficiency measure is accepted footage per production session. A faster model that creates more unusable takes may cost more time overall. Track rejected takes and the reasons for rejection before changing models or increasing concurrency.

10. Derive Shorts from the accepted film

Choose excerpts that contain a complete visual idea: a reveal, an arrival, a short action, or a change in the world. Reframe deliberately for vertical output. A centered crop can remove the destination, the feet, or the object that makes the action understandable.

Elsewhere's vertical edits reuse the accepted picture and soundtrack. Review the new crop, text placement, entrance, and ending as a separate edit. Keep a clean version as well as any version carrying a short hook or invitation to the full film. Captions belong where there is speech or useful context; an instrumental film does not need invented narration.

Watch the export at phone size with the platform's interface area in mind. Keep the important action visible, and listen to the actual exported audio. A short excerpt can expose a rough music boundary that was unnoticeable inside a longer cue.

Publication adds another review: correct file, title, thumbnail, links, visibility, processing, and playback. Follow the platform's current disclosure requirements. Local generation and an original prompt do not settle every source or usage question; retain the provenance and applicable licenses for the material you use.

Measure the audience response separately from production quality. Compare retention and traffic sources at similar release ages where possible. A Short's views do not prove that viewers continued to the full film, and a small audience sample does not establish why one opening performed differently.

Your first local film

Make the first deliverable small enough to finish:

  1. Write one paragraph describing a place, an action, and an ending.
  2. Select a small set of locally sourced plates that agree about the world.
  3. Prove the hardest action in one native motion take.
  4. Build six distinct five-second shots with consistent technical settings.
  5. Select or compose a local 30-second soundtrack and shape its ending.
  6. Assemble, probe, decode, watch, and listen to the complete export.
  7. Preserve the accepted version before trying a longer film or a vertical cut.

The lasting part of the Elsewhere workflow is the ability to inspect and revise each decision. You can replace a model, change an editor, or improve the hardware while keeping that method: define the experience, test its hardest part, preserve what works, and judge the film that the viewer will actually see.
